James Anderson: Thank you, Doctor. Yeah, it was a big milestone. Feeling it a bit in the knees, but otherwise hanging in there.

Dr. Chen: Glad to hear it. So, we're here for your quarterly follow-up for the diabetes and blood pressure. How have you been feeling generally? Any dizziness, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

Dr. Chen: I understand, celebrations happen. But we want to get that back under 7.0 to protect your kidneys and eyes, and to help with that neuropathy in your toes. Are you taking the Metformin regularly?

James Anderson: Yes, 1000 milligrams twice a day with breakfast and dinner. I never miss it.

Dr. Chen: Good. And the Lisinopril?

James Anderson: That's the 20 milligrams, right? Yeah, every morning.

Dr. Chen: Correct. And are you still taking the Atorvastatin for cholesterol?

James Anderson: Yes, the 40 milligrams at bedtime.

Dr. Chen: Excellent. Your LDL looks great, by the way, down to 85. So the statin is doing its job. Given the A1c rise, I'm not going to change your medication yet. I want to give you three months to tighten up the diet. Cut back on the processed sugars, white bread, and pasta. If it's still above 7.5 next time, we might discuss adding a medication like Empagliflozin.

James Anderson: Okay, I really don't want another pill if I can avoid it. I'll get back on the wagon.

James Anderson: Alright.

Dr. Chen: Can you feel this filament?

James Anderson: Yes, but it feels a bit dull near the big toe compared to the heel.

Dr. Chen: Okay. You have some mild peripheral neuropathy developing. It's crucial you check your feet daily for any cuts, sores, or redness that isn't healing. Tight glucose control will help stop this from getting worse.

James Anderson: Understood. I'll be careful.

Dr. Chen: I'm sending refills for the Metformin, Lisinopril, and Atorvastatin to your pharmacy. I also want you to schedule your annual diabetic eye exam; I don't see a report in your chart for this year.

James Anderson: Oh right, I forgot to book that. I'll call the ophthalmologist today.

Dr. Chen: Perfect. Let's recheck that blood pressure... Okay, 132 over 82. Much better. Keep logging your home readings. I'll see you in three months, James.

James Anderson: Thanks, Dr. Chen. See you then.

Doctor: Good morning, Linda. It is good to see you again. Happy belated birthday—I see you just turned 50 last week.

Linda Wilson: Thank you, Doctor. Yes, it was a big milestone. I’m trying to embrace the new decade.

Doctor: That’s the right attitude. We are here for your annual thyroid follow-up today. I’ve reviewed the blood work you had drawn at the lab last Tuesday, but before we go over the numbers, I want to hear how you are feeling. How have your energy levels been?

Linda Wilson: To be honest, I’ve been dragging a bit lately. I thought it might just be age or work stress, but even after a full night's sleep, I wake up feeling tired. By 2:00 PM, I feel like I need a nap.

Doctor: I see. And how long has this fatigue been noticeable?

Linda Wilson: Probably about three or four months now. It’s been gradual.

Doctor: Have you noticed any other changes? Specifically regarding your weight, hair, or skin?

Linda Wilson: Yes, actually. My skin has been incredibly dry, mostly on my arms and legs. And I’ve gained about eight pounds since my last visit, even though my diet hasn't really changed. It’s been frustrating.

Doctor: I can imagine. What about temperature sensitivity? Do you feel colder than usual?

Linda Wilson: Definitely. My husband keeps the house at 72, and I’m sitting there in a sweater and a blanket.

Doctor: Okay. Let's review your medication adherence. You are currently prescribed Levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily. How are you taking that?

Linda Wilson: I take it first thing in the morning, right when I wake up, with water.

Doctor: Do you eat immediately after?

Linda Wilson: No, I usually walk the dog and shower, so it’s at least 45 minutes to an hour before I have breakfast or coffee.

Doctor: Excellent. That’s exactly how you should take it. Do you take any other supplements?

Linda Wilson: Just a multivitamin and Vitamin D, but I take those with dinner.

Doctor: Good, so no interference with absorption there. Let's look at your vitals. Your blood pressure is 118/76, which is great. Heart rate is 62—a little on the lower side of normal. Now, looking at your labs: your TSH level came back at 7.4 mIU/L, and your Free T4 is 0.8 ng/dL.

Linda Wilson: That TSH sounds high. It was around 2 last year, right?

Doctor: Exactly. A TSH of 7.4 indicates that your hypothyroidism is not currently well-controlled on the current dose. Your pituitary gland is working overtime trying to stimulate the thyroid. This explains the fatigue, the weight gain, the dry skin, and the cold intolerance. You are clinically hypothyroid right now.

Linda Wilson: Well, at least there is a reason for how I'm feeling. What do we do?

Doctor: We need to increase your dosage. The 75 micrograms isn't quite enough anymore. I am going to bump you up to Levothyroxine 88 micrograms daily. 

Linda Wilson: Okay.

Doctor: It’s a small increase, but it should be enough to get your TSH back down into the ideal range of 0.5 to 2.5. I'm sending the prescription to your pharmacy now. 

Linda Wilson: Should I finish the old bottle first?

Doctor: How many do you have left?

Linda Wilson: Maybe a week's worth.

Doctor: Go ahead and start the new 88 microgram dose tomorrow morning. You can hold onto the old ones as a backup just in case, but let's get you on the therapeutic dose immediately so you can start feeling better.

Linda Wilson: Sounds good. When will I feel a difference?

Doctor: You might notice a little more energy in about two weeks, but it takes a full 6 to 8 weeks for the levels to stabilize in your blood. Because of this change, I need to see you back sooner than a year. I want you to get lab work done again in 8 weeks.

Linda Wilson: Okay, I can do that.

Doctor: We need to make sure we don't swing you too far the other way into hyperthyroidism. If you start feeling a racing heart, anxiety, or trouble sleeping, call me immediately. Otherwise, I'll see you in two months to review the new labs.

Linda Wilson: Thank you, Doctor. I really hope this helps with the energy.

Doctor: I am confident it will. Take care, Linda.

Betty Lewis: I didn't realize it would make that much of a difference. I'll cut back to my usual amount.

Dr. Evans: That would be helpful. Before we decide on the dose change, I want to run through a few questions. Have you noticed any unusual bruising, bleeding gums when brushing, or nosebleeds?

Betty Lewis: No, nothing like that.

Dr. Evans: Any dark or tarry stools? Or blood in the urine?

Betty Lewis: No, everything is normal there.

Betty Lewis: Yes, once a day in the morning.

Dr. Evans: And the Atorvastatin for cholesterol?

Betty Lewis: Yes, 20 milligrams at bedtime.

Dr. Evans: Have you taken any over-the-counter medications? Ibuprofen, aspirin, or nutritional supplements?

Betty Lewis: Just Tylenol occasionally for my knee pain. I know I’m not supposed to take Advil.

Betty Lewis: That’s good to hear.

Dr. Evans: I’m checking your ankles for swelling... trace edema, but nothing concerning. No signs of deep vein thrombosis.

Dr. Evans: Good morning, Mr. King. Good to see you again. How have you been feeling since our last visit three months ago?

George King: Well, Doctor, I'm hanging in there. The legs are still giving me some trouble, though. I'm 64 now, and I feel like I'm slowing down faster than I should be.

Dr. Evans: I understand. Let's talk about the legs. Are you still experiencing that cramping pain in your calves when you walk?

George King: Yeah, it's mostly the right calf. It starts acting up after I walk about two blocks or so. It feels tight, like a charley horse that won't let go until I stop moving.

Dr. Evans: And does it resolve quickly once you rest?

George King: Usually takes about five minutes of sitting on a bench, and then I can go again. But it's frustrating. I used to be able to walk the dog around the whole park.

Dr. Evans: That sounds like classic intermittent claudication, consistent with your Peripheral Artery Disease diagnosis. Have you noticed any pain while you're resting, specifically at night in bed? Do your feet hurt when they are elevated?

George King: No, thankfully. Once I'm off my feet, the pain is gone. I sleep fine.

Dr. Evans: That is a very good sign. It means the blood flow isn't critically compromised yet. Now, George, we have to touch on the most important factor here. How is the smoking cessation going?

George King: I know, I know. I’m trying. I was at a pack a day, and now I’m down to maybe five or six cigarettes. It's hard, Doc. I've been smoking since I was eighteen.

Dr. Evans: I give you credit for cutting down, but with PAD, every single cigarette causes vasoconstriction—it tightens those blood vessels and makes it harder for blood to get to your legs. We really need to get you to zero. Are you using the nicotine patches we discussed?

George King: I forget to put them on sometimes. But I'll try harder.

Dr. Evans: Please do. It’s the single best thing you can do to save your legs. Let's review your medications. You are taking the Clopidogrel 75 milligrams daily, correct?

George King: The Plavix? Yes, I take that every morning with my breakfast. And the baby Aspirin.

Dr. Evans: Excellent. That dual antiplatelet therapy is crucial to prevent clots. I also see you're on Atorvastatin 80 milligrams for your cholesterol. Any muscle aches from that?

George King: No, that one seems fine.

Dr. Evans: Good. High-intensity statins stabilize the plaque in your arteries. I'm going to take a look at your feet now. Please slip off your shoes and socks.

[Sound of movement]

Dr. Evans: Okay... skin looks a bit shiny and hairless on the lower shins, which is typical for PAD. No open sores or ulcers, which is excellent. I'm checking the pulses now. The dorsalis pedis is palpable but weak on the right, about 1-plus. The posterior tibial is also diminished. Capillary refill is about 3 seconds. Your feet are a little cool to the touch, but not cold.

George King: Is that bad?

Dr. Evans: It's stable. It hasn't gotten significantly worse since last time. Here is the plan: We are going to continue the Clopidogrel and Aspirin. I want you to really focus on the walking program. Walk until the pain is moderate, stop and rest until it goes away, and then walk again. This helps build collateral circulation—new pathways for blood flow.

George King: Walk through the pain?

Dr. Evans: Walk until it hurts, stop, recover, repeat. Do that for 30 minutes a day. And George, we need to get serious about quitting the cigarettes completely. I'm going to refill your prescription for the patches. I want to see you back in three months, but call me immediately if you develop any sores on your feet that won't heal or if you have pain while resting.

George King: Alright, Doctor. I'll stick with it.

Dr. Evans: Take care, Mr. King.

Michelle Baker: Hi, Dr. Evans. Honestly, I’m feeling quite a bit better. I'm not nearly as exhausted as I was back in January. I used to need a nap every afternoon just to get through the day, but now I can usually power through until bedtime.

Dr. Evans: That is excellent to hear. Improved energy levels are usually the first sign that the treatment is working. How about the shortness of breath you mentioned? You said you were getting winded climbing the stairs to your apartment.

Michelle Baker: It’s still there a little bit if I rush, but I can carry groceries up the stairs now without feeling like I’m going to pass out. So, definitely an improvement.

Dr. Evans: Good. And the ice cravings? The pica?

Michelle Baker: Gone, thankfully. I haven't had the urge to chew ice in weeks. My husband is relieved; the crunching was driving him crazy.

Dr. Evans: That’s a very specific symptom of iron deficiency, so the fact that it resolved is a great clinical sign. Let’s talk about the medication. You are taking the Ferrous Sulfate 325 mg, correct?

Michelle Baker: Yes, 325 milligrams, once a day.

Dr. Evans: Have you been able to take it consistently?

Michelle Baker: mostly. I missed maybe two or three days when I went out of town and forgot the bottle, but otherwise, I take it every morning.

Dr. Evans: How are you tolerating it? We discussed that it can be tough on the stomach.

Michelle Baker: It was rough at first. I had some nausea and pretty bad constipation for the first two weeks. I almost stopped taking it.

Dr. Evans: I'm glad you didn't. Did you try the stool softener we discussed?

Michelle Baker: Yes, I bought some Colace, and that helped. I also started drinking a lot more water. The nausea went away once I started taking the pill with a little bit of food, although I know you said an empty stomach is better.

Dr. Evans: Ideally, yes, empty stomach is best for absorption. However, if taking it with a small amount of food helps you stay compliant, that is better than not taking it at all. Just avoid dairy or calcium supplements within two hours of the iron. Are you still taking it with orange juice?

Michelle Baker: Yes, I drink a small glass of OJ with it every time. You said the Vitamin C helps.

Dr. Evans: Exactly. It creates an acidic environment that helps your body absorb the iron. Now, let’s look at your labs from yesterday. Your Hemoglobin has come up from 9.2 to 11.5. That is fantastic progress. It’s not quite in the normal range yet—we want you above 12—but it’s a big jump.

Michelle Baker: Oh, that’s a relief.

Dr. Evans: Your Ferritin, which measures your iron stores, is up to 18 ng/mL. It was at 4 previously. This is still on the lower side, which explains why you aren't back to 100% energy yet, but it’s moving in the right direction. It takes a long time to refill those iron stores.

Michelle Baker: So, do I need to keep taking the pills?

Dr. Evans: Yes, Michelle. I want you to continue the Ferrous Sulfate 325 mg daily for at least another three months. If the constipation flares up again, keep using the docusate sodium. I also want to briefly touch on diet again. How has that been going?

Michelle Baker: I’m trying. I’m eating red meat twice a week, usually lean beef. And I’ve been making salads with spinach instead of iceberg lettuce. I also started eating fortified cereal for breakfast.

Dr. Evans: That sounds perfect. The heme iron from the meat is the easiest for your body to use, but the spinach and fortified grains help too. Just remember, tea and coffee can block iron absorption, so try to have those between meals rather than with your iron-rich meals.

Michelle Baker: Okay, I didn't know that about coffee. I’ll watch out for that.

Dr. Evans: Great. Let's listen to your heart and lungs really quick... (Sounds of movement)... Deep breath... Good. Heart rate is 78, regular rhythm. No murmurs. Lungs are clear. Your conjunctiva—the inner eyelid—looks much pinker than last time. You were very pale before.

Michelle Baker: I feel like I have my color back too.

Dr. Evans: You certainly do. Okay, the plan is simple: continue the iron supplements, keep up the dietary changes, and we will repeat the CBC and Ferritin panel in 3 months. If you start feeling fatigued again or have any black, tarry stools unrelated to the iron, call me immediately.

Michelle Baker: Will do. Thanks, Dr. Evans.

Dr. Aris: Good morning, Gary. Good to see you again. I see we’re celebrating a birthday soon, you'll be turning 59 in December?

Gary Turner: That’s right, Dr. Aris. Holding steady at 58 for a few more months. Feeling pretty good, honestly.

Dr. Aris: Glad to hear it. Today is our annual follow-up to monitor your liver function following your Hepatitis C cure. It’s been, what, four years now since you finished treatment?

Gary Turner: Yeah, about four years since I finished the Epclusa. Best thing I ever did.

Dr. Aris: Absolutely. I pulled up your labs from earlier this week. The great news is that your HCV RNA quantitative test remains undetectable. That means you have maintained your Sustained Virologic Response. You are still officially cured of the virus.

Gary Turner: That’s always a relief to hear. I still worry it might come back.

Dr. Aris: Reinfection is only possible if you are exposed to the virus again through blood-to-blood contact. Spontaneous recurrence is virtually unheard of. Now, let’s look at the liver enzymes. Your ALT is 29 and AST is 25. These are perfectly within the normal range. Your platelets are 180, which is good; it suggests we aren't seeing signs of significant portal hypertension or scarring progression.

Gary Turner: So, no cirrhosis?

Dr. Aris: Based on your last elastography scan and these numbers, you have some mild fibrosis—scarring—from the years you had the virus, but you do not have cirrhosis. However, because you had the infection for a long time, we still need to be vigilant. I noticed on your chart you're still taking Lisinopril 10mg for blood pressure and Atorvastatin 20mg for cholesterol?

Gary Turner: Yes, taking those every morning. My GP actually bumped the Atorvastatin up to 20mg last month because my LDL was creeping up.

Dr. Aris: That’s fine. Statins are generally safe for the liver and can actually be protective. I do want to ask about alcohol use. Be honest with me, Gary.

Gary Turner: I’ll have a beer or two during the football game on Sundays. Nothing heavy. I know I shouldn't.

Dr. Aris: With the history of Hep C and the mild scarring we know is there, zero alcohol is really the gold standard. Alcohol is a direct toxin to the liver cells. Plus, the ultrasound showed some mild fatty infiltration—hepatic steatosis. Alcohol contributes to that, as does diet.

Gary Turner: I've been trying to cut down on the fried stuff. I’ve put on a few pounds around the middle.

Dr. Aris: Weight loss will help the fatty liver significantly. I’d like you to aim for losing about 5 to 10 pounds before our next visit. Also, for pain relief, are you taking anything? Headaches, joint pain?

Gary Turner: Just Tylenol occasionally. I stay away from Advil like you told me.

Dr. Aris: Good. Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs can cause bleeding issues or kidney stress, which we want to avoid. Acetaminophen is safe, just keep it under 2,000 milligrams a day. Do not mix it with alcohol.

Gary Turner: Understood.

Dr. Aris: Okay, I’m going to order a surveillance ultrasound for six months from now just to screen for hepatocellular carcinoma. It’s standard protocol for patients with your history of fibrosis. Keep up with the Lisinopril and Atorvastatin, and let’s really try to eliminate those Sunday beers.

Gary Turner: Will do, Doc. See you in six months.

Normally, if calcium is high, your body should shut off PTH production. The fact that both are high confirms the diagnosis of Primary Hyperparathyroidism.

Eugene Long: So it is the gland acting up.

Dr. Evans: Exactly. We also got the results back from your DEXA scan. It shows osteopenia, particularly in the distal radius of the forearm. Eugene Long: You think it's time for surgery?

Dr. Evans: I do. We ordered the Sestamibi parathyroid scan last week to see if we could localize the problem. The images showed a distinct uptake in the lower right pole of the thyroid bed. This suggests a single parathyroid adenoma—a benign growth—rather than all four glands being enlarged. This is good news because it makes the surgery much more straightforward, usually minimally invasive.

Eugene Long: Okay. I was hoping to avoid it, but if it stops the stones and helps the tiredness, I'm in. What do I do about my meds in the meantime?

My girlfriend mentioned that the whites of my eyes looked a little yellow. It freaked me out a bit. It went away once I started eating again, but I wanted to make sure my liver isn't failing or something.

Dr. Sarah Miller: I understand why that would be alarming, but let me reassure you immediately—your liver is not failing. I've reviewed your Comprehensive Metabolic Panel, and it actually aligns perfectly with what you’re describing and your history of Gilbert's syndrome.

Tyler Hayes: Okay, that's a relief. So the yellowing was just the Gilbert's?

Dr. Sarah Miller: Exactly. Let's look at the numbers. Your liver enzymes—the AST and ALT—are completely normal. AST is 22 and ALT is 24. If there was liver damage or hepatitis, we'd see those numbers spike into the hundreds or thousands. However, your Total Bilirubin is elevated at 2.4 mg/dL, and your Direct Bilirubin is normal at 0.3. This means the elevation is almost entirely 'indirect' or unconjugated bilirubin.

Tyler Hayes: Right, the stuff my liver is slow at processing?

Dr. Sarah Miller: Precisely. In Gilbert's syndrome, you have a genetic variant that makes the enzyme responsible for processing bilirubin slightly less efficient. It usually handles normal loads fine, but when your body is under stress—like that viral illness you mentioned, or the fasting caused by not eating—the enzyme falls behind, and bilirubin builds up in the blood. That causes the mild scleral icterus, or yellowing of the eyes.

Tyler Hayes: Okay. I’ve also been doing some heavy weightlifting and taking Ibuprofen for soreness. Does that affect it?

Dr. Sarah Miller: Vigorous exercise can sometimes be a mild trigger due to the physical stress on the body, but it's generally fine. Ibuprofen is processed by the kidneys mostly, so it's not a major issue for the liver in standard doses, though I'd recommend sticking to Acetaminophen if you have stomach sensitivity, just don't exceed 3000mg a day. But for Gilbert's specifically, the main triggers are fasting, illness, dehydration, and lack of sleep.

Tyler Hayes: Got it. So, do I need to take anything for it? Or change my diet?

Dr. Sarah Miller: No treatment is needed. Gilbert's is considered a benign condition. It doesn't lead to chronic liver disease or fibrosis. My plan for you is simply reassurance and annual monitoring. You don't need a special diet, but you should avoid prolonged fasting or crash diets, as those will likely bring the jaundice back. Just stay hydrated and eat regular meals.

Tyler Hayes: That sounds easy enough. I was worried I'd need to stop drinking alcohol entirely.

Dr. Sarah Miller: You don't need to abstain completely, but moderation is always key for general health. Your liver is healthy, Tyler. 

Tyler Hayes: Thanks, Dr. Miller. That really puts my mind at ease.

Amanda Green: Yes, please. I just want to get it fixed.

Amanda Green: Ugh, okay. Is that an STD? Did I get this from my boyfriend?

Dr. Reynolds: That is a very common question. BV is not considered a sexually transmitted infection in the traditional sense. It's caused by an overgrowth of bacteria that are normally present in the vagina, specifically when the healthy Lactobacilli bacteria get outnumbered by other bacteria like Gardnerella. Amanda Green: Okay, that’s a relief. So, does he need to take medicine?

Amanda Green: I can definitely add more yogurt to my diet.

Dr. Reynolds: Also, avoid douching. I know the odor makes you want to wash inside, but douching actually flushes out the good bacteria and makes BV worse. Just use warm water and mild, unscented soap on the outside.
